candidates.title: The Gas Remembers
candidates.pitch: A visitor types a word and about 1,500 coloured particles spell it out; a gas simulation then scatters it into confetti while an entropy meter climbs. Pressing rewind runs the same laws backwards and the word re-forms, sealed by a bit-for-bit return receipt, because integer arithmetic makes every step exactly undoable. Switching to ordinary floating point, or nudging one particle by one part in a million, breaks the return, and a V-shaped mismatch curve points to the moment and the particle of the nudge.
candidates.whyNow: Timeless. The arrow-of-time puzzle is about 150 years old, yet a toy that lets anyone break the reversal by hand is rare, and clips of dye unmixing in glycerin keep circulating (one was fact-checked as authentic).

research.summary: Time-symmetric dynamics would retrace their path when every velocity is flipped; Loschmidt raised this against Boltzmann's H-theorem and Boltzmann answered that reversed states exist but are overwhelmingly rare. Floating-point simulations rarely manage it: the forward-and-back error grows exponentially in chaotic systems. Levesque and Verlet (1993) described an integer-arithmetic scheme that is exactly reversible, and later bit-reversible integrators use the same idea. University demos of dye unmixing in glycerin show the physical cousin. Scout prototype, not literature: 400 soft disks on a 2^20 integer lattice with antisymmetric rounded pair forces returned bit-exactly after 1500 steps out and 1500 back; a one-unit nudge grew by a factor e every 8 to 27 steps depending on density, and the mismatch against the clean replay had its apex at the nudge step. Model limits: 2D soft disks, a small gas, coarse-grained entropy, no quantum effects; Lyapunov rates are measured in the page and depend on its parameters.

sources.title: Loschmidt's paradox
sources.snippet: Entry on the reversibility objection: because microscopic laws are time-symmetric, reversing all velocities after entropy has risen would send a gas back toward lower entropy; Boltzmann replied that such states are extremely rare.
sources.note: Established the objection and Boltzmann's statistical reply; the 1876 date appeared in two separate search summaries (summaries blended several results, entry itself not opened).

sources.note: Second, independent account of the objection; no date is taken from it because its early date was flagged as doubtful.

sources.title: JANUS: A bit-wise reversible integrator for N-body dynamics
sources.snippet: Introduces a bit-wise reversible N-body integrator that combines integer and floating-point arithmetic so that forward and backward integration agree exactly.
sources.note: Later work building on integer reversibility; shows the idea is still used.

sources.title: Time's Arrow for Shockwaves; Bit-Reversible Lyapunov and 'Covariant' Vectors; Symmetry Breaking
sources.snippet: Shockwave study with about 1600 particles using bit-reversible integration and exact velocity reversal at set times; forward and backward Lyapunov exponents converge to machine accuracy yet differ from each other.
sources.note: Shows bit-reversible runs used in practice for time-reversal studies.

sources.title: ANALYSIS OF ROUND OFF ERRORS WITH REVERSIBILITY TEST AS A DYNAMICAL INDICATOR
sources.snippet: Proposes using the round-off deviation after a forward-and-back integration as a dynamical indicator; the reversibility error grows exponentially for chaotic orbits and only linearly for regular ones.
sources.note: Established exponential growth of reversal error in chaos versus linear growth in regular motion.

facts.claim: Loschmidt's reversibility objection (reported as 1876): because microscopic laws are time-symmetric, reversing every velocity after entropy has risen would send a gas back toward lower entropy; Boltzmann replied that such reversed states exist but are extremely rare.
Levesque and Verlet published 'Molecular dynamics and time reversibility' (J. Stat. Phys. 72, 519-537, 1993), describing a time-symmetric integer-arithmetic algorithm for simulating classical fluids.

Bit-reversible integrators are used in published work: a 2017 N-body integrator (JANUS) mixes integer and floating-point arithmetic for exact time reversal, and a shockwave study with about 1600 particles reverses velocities exactly in bit-reversible runs.
Round-off prevents exact numerical reversal in molecular dynamics, and the error of a forward-and-back run grows exponentially for chaotic orbits but only linearly for regular ones.

Dye lines in glycerol between two cylinders un-mix when the rotation is reversed, a standard university lecture demonstration (with a recommended limit on the number of turns), and a viral clip of one such demonstration was fact-checked as authentic.

inspirations: git bisect as a debugging idiom

design.coreLoop: The visitor chooses a word, lets the gas disperse it, rewinds time and reads the return receipt, which compares the final state with the start bit for bit. The visitor then breaks the echo on purpose, with a nudge, a hornet particle (one very fast particle) or floating-point arithmetic, and the mismatch curve shows when and where it broke. A hidden-nudge hunt scores how few rewinds it takes to find the moment and the particle, so minute two is about experiments and minute ten is about forensics and the bits bench.
sophisticationHooks: Exactly reversible integer Stormer-Verlet core with antisymmetric rounded pair forces (momentum conserved exactly), run side by side with float64 and float32 builds of the same code; a Node test asserts the bit-exact return.

Echo forensics: the distance between the clean replay and the reversed replay is zero just before a nudge and grows both ways, a V on a log axis whose apex marks the moment and the one particle that differs.
Bits bench in a worker: repeated one-unit nudges at several lattice resolutions measure the echo horizon against the page's own Lyapunov rate.

Coarse-grained entropy meter whose arrow flips at the rewind, collision ticks that play backwards on rewind, and a share hash that replays the same universe on any device (IEEE add, multiply, divide and square root only).
design.scopeForOneDay: The day builds a pure deterministic engine (init, step, reverse, hash, entropy) with Node tests for exact return and momentum, a canvas renderer for 800 to 1500 particles with cell lists, rewind and scrub controls, the return receipt, mismatch and entropy plots, nudge and hornet tools, the hidden-nudge hunt, the bits bench, a share hash, an about panel, light and dark themes, a reduced-motion step-through, keyboard and touch. The day cuts 3D, event-driven hard spheres, a fluid-unmixing mode, quantum echoes and any server.
risks: Defaults decide whether float64 fails before the gas has visibly mixed; the scout prototype showed float64 returns holding for roughly 600 to 1000 steps and failing between about 800 and 1400 steps, depending on density and speed, so tuned parameters and a visible step counter are needed.
Cross-device replay depends on using only IEEE add, multiply, divide and square root in the force path; Math.exp, Math.pow or trigonometry there would break the shared-state promise.
Phones: 1500 particles need cell lists and a cap on steps per frame; reduced-motion visitors need a step-through mode instead of continuous animation.

Lyapunov rates and echo horizons shown on the page are measured from its own model and labelled as such; only the verified literature facts are cited, and the making-of uses 'reported' wording for anything else.
Letters can lose legibility after the return, so long words or thin glyphs need a fallback shape or fewer characters.
The physical analogue (dye in glycerol) fails once diffusion intervenes, so the page states what is modelled (exact arithmetic) and what is not, and does not suggest that real gases un-mix.

candidates.title: The Shortcut Trap
candidates.pitch: A weight hangs from two springs and a few strings, and a visitor predicts whether snipping the short linking string will drop or lift it; the weight rises, against intuition. Sliders for string length and spring stiffness reveal the narrow band where this happens, a bounce metronome shows the weight vibrating twice as fast after the cut, and a mapping toggle recasts the same network as roads where closing a free shortcut cuts everyone's commute from 80 to 65 minutes in the textbook case. A puzzle mode deals random networks with a cut budget and scores the lift against the best possible.
candidates.whyNow: Timeless. Road-closure and induced-demand arguments keep returning, and the spring version of the Braess paradox keeps resurfacing in physics lecture demos and blogs (posts from 2025 and 2026 turned up in search).

research.summary: In 1991 Cohen and Horowitz published a string-and-spring network in which cutting a string that supports a weight makes the weight rise, with an electrical analogue and a traffic analogy; it is formally the Braess paradox (1968), where adding a free road raises every driver's travel time. With the linking string intact the two springs act in series (k/2) while two longer safety strings hang slack; after the cut the safety strings take over and the springs act in parallel (2k), so the weight sits higher by W/(2k) minus an offset (read by the scout as the slack left in the safety strings). Scout check, not literature: a small static solver for equal springs, load F, stiffness k gave a lift that peaks at F/(2k), is positive only inside a band of safety-string lengths of width F/k, and is negative above it. Textbook traffic version: 4000 drivers, 65 minutes becoming 80 after a free link. Model limits: ideal massless springs, inextensible strings, quasi-static equilibrium, linear latencies, selfish routing; the paradox needs those conditions and the page says so.

facts.claim: Cohen and Horowitz (Nature 352, 699-701, 22 August 1991) described a string-and-spring network in which cutting a string that supports a weight makes the weight rise at equilibrium, with an electrical analogue and a traffic analogy.

With the linking string intact the two springs act in series (effective stiffness k/2) and the secondary strings hang slack; after the cut the secondary strings take the load and the springs act in parallel (2k, four times stiffer), so each spring carries half the weight and the weight sits higher.

The net rise is W/(2k) minus the original stretch, so the effect exists only when that stretch is smaller than W/(2k); a small amount of slack in the strings cannot make up for the reduced spring extension, so the mass ends up higher.

University lecture-demo collections list the demonstration: a catalogue entry named Spring and String Thing (B4-04) described as a counterintuitive series-and-parallel demo, and a demo page titled Spring Paradox (B17).

In the textbook Braess network (credited to Dietrich Braess, 1968), 4000 drivers choose between two routes, each a leg taking T/100 minutes (T = drivers on it) plus a fixed 45-minute leg; an even split takes 65 minutes, while a free link between the midpoints sends everyone over both congestible legs for 80 minutes and no one gains by switching back.

Reported, not confirmed: commonly cited real-world cases are Stuttgart (1969, a new downtown street worsened congestion and was closed), Seoul (Cheonggyecheon expressway removal, about 2003-2005) and New York (42nd Street closed for Earth Day 1990 without the predicted gridlock); sources differ on details.
Reported, not confirmed: lecture slides state that the paradox arises under selfish (user-optimal) routing and does not arise when a planner assigns system-optimal routes.

design.coreLoop: Each round shows a spring-and-string network with a cut budget. The visitor predicts rise, fall or no change, snips a string, and a physics relaxation settles to a measured height change that is scored against the prediction. A why-overlay colours taut and slack elements and shows series or parallel stiffness; a mapping toggle shows the same network as roads with a commute readout. Replay value comes from a daily seeded puzzle scored against the optimal cut set, sliders that move the paradox band, and networks where two cuts beat any single cut.
sophisticationHooks: Tension-only strings and linear springs solved with XPBD plus a final settle, unit-tested against the closed form for the classic arrangement (lift equals F/(2k) minus the slack left in the secondary strings, the scout's reading of the original stretch).

A live phase strip under the sliders draws lift against secondary-string length as a tent for the equal-spring arrangement (positive inside a band of width F/k, peak F/(2k), negative beyond), produced by the same solver as the scene.

A seeded network generator that guarantees at least one counterintuitive cut and brute-forces the optimal cut set for the par score; bounce sonification doubles in rate after the cut because stiffness quadruples.
A road-map toggle that solves a user-equilibrium traffic assignment on the mapped network, so the cut reads as a road closure with before and after commute times.
design.scopeForOneDay: The day builds the XPBD core with closed-form tests, scissors interaction, six hand-made levels plus the seeded generator with brute-force par, the phase strip, bounce sonification, prediction scoring, the road-map toggle with a small equilibrium solver, a share hash, an about panel, light and dark themes, reduced motion (instant settle), keyboard and touch. The day cuts user-built networks, 3D, and the electrical and hydraulic analogues (named in the about panel only).
risks: A quick Newton prototype of the static solver diverged for one very long secondary string, so the real solver needs a monotone method (XPBD with a final settle, or an active-set solve) and tests for slack and taut transitions.
The paradox exists only inside a band of parameters; the copy states that cutting lifts the weight only inside a band, and the sliders show both sides.
Real-world road cases come from popular articles and slides with differing details, so they appear as reported with a date, or are left out.
The price-of-anarchy bound of 4/3 for linear latencies was recalled from memory and not confirmed in search, so the page shows only measured ratios.
Spring-and-string demos already exist as lecture demos and videos, so the page differentiates through prediction scoring, the phase strip, the generator and the road mapping.
The traffic model (linear latencies, selfish routing, one origin-destination pair) is a toy, and the page says it is not traffic-planning advice.
